questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer:
To me, it was very important that I received my education in a language which I feel comfortable with, which is why I in the first place looked at UK. I am only very well reading and speaking in English and Danish, so this very much affected my choice.

Secondly, I was very aware of the Anthropological history UoM, and I quickly found out by researching the university that their Department of Anthropology is still very big. This meant that I had a lot of different courses to choose from, which was also nice. It was important to me that I found courses which were interesting to me, and UoM had pretty much anything an anthropology student could wish for.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The academic part of the stay was great. However, I had a terrible living situation which influenced the overall enjoyment of my stay.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: It was pretty easy, as soon as I had attached my email to a student account at Manchester I received a lot of e-mail with information regarding my start there. I was not informed that single-semester exchange students are not offered student housing through the UNI. I was not informed about this before I wrote their accommodation department, which was very disappointing.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: We had an intro-meeting with an ERASMUS coordinator, and were pointed in different directions to receive campus tours, join communities and so on. Overall the student center and help you could get there was great. I almost never felt in need of more information, and when I did, it was usually. easy to find.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: It was very difficult. As mentioned, the uni does not offer student housing to single-semester exchanges. There is a housing crisis in the UK (2023), and it is also bad in Manchester where there are a lot of students/young professionals fighting for housing. Landlords and solicitors are hard to find and when you do come across them, they seem sketchy. It is very easy for them to find people, so it is difficult to complain about the conditions of the shit-hole houses many of them let.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: The state of the rooms and common areas in the old town houses, which make up most of the Manchurian landscape, is in shambles. The buildings are old and usually just used by speculators to rake in insane amounts of rent from young people who have no where else to go. The people letting usually don't live in the house which they let, so no one living there will care about upholding a decent common area. You are not very well protected, like you are in Denmark for example, so it is very difficult to file complaints of these shadow-landlords, and much of the time, it is just easier to find another place to stay it seems. I have never heard of anyone in Manchester actually getting anything back on their deposit, so beware.

Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: This part was decently easy, I just had to write which classes I wanted to a coordinator who contacted  me. When I did it wrong, she tried to help me.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: A coordinator was there to help.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I was not registered for any classes upon arrival, but this was quickly fixed by people at the uni when I wrote them. Even though some of the classes I had asked to be in had been 'filled' due to the registration being open for local students, I was put in these classes. So do not fear, they were very accommodating in this regard.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Try to check through the host-institutions student-net service whether you have been enrolled in classes or not as soon as you have access.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The level was high, which was what I desired. The staff expects a lot of you, and there is a lot of reading, but if you are ready to put in the work, you will get so much great education in return.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: It was pretty similar, although most classes did not have the portfolio-type of assessments as we do at UCPH. It depends a lot on the teacher as well, as the teaching staff is very diverse in gender and nationalities. The teachers did a lot of extra-curricular events which were nice.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Anthropology of Visions, Senses and Memories
Anthropology of Displacement and Migration
Screening Culture

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
All of the above. They were all great.
Visions was a course centered around phenomenological and sensual approaches in anthropology, both theoretically and methodically, as ways of generating knowledge with interlocutors. Andrew Irving teaches the course, and is a very inspiring and laid-back character with a lot of research on his resume.

Displacement and Migration was a great course which centered around different themes of migration. Sebastien Bachelet was teaching the course at the time, and was a great educator. 

Screening Culture takes you through all of the main ideas, theories, themes and methods of filmmaking within the anthropological genre. A great course if you are interested in filmmaking as an anthropological tool.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Not any, really. I rented a bicycle for the months I was there which saved me a lot on bus-fares. Manchester is a very decent city to cycle around.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Food is not cheap. Also, heating was included in my rent, but some of my fellow students got slapped with gas charges in the winter.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I did not use any of these much

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: All sorts of sports-stuff. The student-union ran a bar where you could meet others.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Student union stuff-

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Visit Liverpool. Eat curries.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It was pretty easy, the English are like the Danes in a lot of ways.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Go to the student bar, also in the daytime. People hang out there. Talk to the people in your classes, they are very talkative and used to exchange students.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: The food culture. They don't cook too much, and so the kitchen where I lived was disgusting and not very well equipped. The alternative is take away, which is mostly really unhealthy food.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Curries. Pub-culture is a sight to behold.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Try to find housing from home.
Prepare to study. A lot. It's great.
Get a bicycle.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Large campus, lots of people. If you want friends, you have to engage others.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The academic outcome of my stay was fantastic.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: My living conditions. Small expensive room, mildew in common areas, very cold and dirty.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
